Begin your evaluation by comparing the assistant's answer against the reference answer in this turn. Be as objective as possible, and provide a detailed justification for your rating. After providing your explanation, you must rate the response on a scale of 1 to 10, strictly following this format: "Rating: [[rating]]", for example: "Rating: [[5]]".

[The Start of Previous Conversation]
user: annual maximum for 401k
assistant: The annual maximum for 401k contributions for 2017 is $54,000, and $53,000 for 2016. This limit includes elective deferrals, employer matching contributions, employer nonelective contributions, and allocations of forfeitures. However, the total annual contributions cannot exceed 100% of the participant's compensation. These limits apply to the total of all of your accounts in plans maintained by one employer (and any related employer). Please note that these limits may change in future years.
user: is this the latest number you have?
assistant: Yes.  I recommend checking the IRS's website for the most recent numbers, as these limits can change over time:  https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/plan-participant-employee/retirement-topics-401k-and-profit-sharing-plan-contribution-limits
user: oh thanks
assistant: You're welcome!   May I help you with something else?
[The End of Previous Conversation]

[The Start of Current Turn Question]
Can I change traditional to Roth without incurring extra tax?
[The End of Current Turn Question]

[The Start of Reference Answer]
You can convert a Traditional IRA to a Roth IRA through a process called recharacterization. However, you will need to report it as a non-deductible Traditional IRA contribution on a Form 8606 Part 1. When you convert, the earnings you have made since contributing will be taxed as income.  If you convert, you will have to fill out Form 8606 Part 2 for the year you convert.
Meanwhile, a traditional 401K is tax-deferred while a Roth 401K has already been taxed so you don't pay taxes on withdrawal (assuming you withdrawal after 59 1/2 years of age). The Roth 401K is advantageous if you believe you'll be in a higher tax bracket than you are currently.  You can also roll over your Roth 401k to a Roth IRA without penalty or additional tax.
[The End of Reference Answer]

[The Start of Assistant's Answer]
Do you mean changing a traditional IRA to a Roth IRA, or a traditional 401(k) to a Roth 401(k)? The documents distinguish recharacterizing an IRA contribution from converting traditional IRA money to Roth. [S2] They describe a “backdoor Roth IRA contribution” involving a nondeductible traditional IRA contribution followed by conversion; if you have no existing pre-tax money in traditional or other IRAs, this achieves the same result as a regular Roth IRA contribution, except without income limits. [S3] However, the evidence does not establish whether your particular change would incur extra tax.
[The End of Assistant's Answer]

Beyond answering your question, I would still like to reiterate that Roth or traditional does not have a big effect on your investment unless you max them out or you have different tax rates now versus in retirement. It may change other things. For example, you can roll over a Roth 401k to a Roth IRA without paying taxes. And the Roth IRA will act like it was contributed directly.

 The earnings would be taxed as regular income, and the earnings may incur a penalty. Yes, you can ""recharacterize"" (all or part of) your Roth IRA contribution as a Traditional IRA contribution (or vice versa) by April 15. Recharacterization means you pretend the contribution was originally made as a Traditional IRA contribution, and did not involve Roth IRA at all. (""Conversion"" is something very different and can only go from Traditional to Roth, not the other way around.) You are likely not eligible to deduct that Traditional IRA contribution, so you will have to report it as a non-deductible Traditional IRA contribution on a 2015 Form 8606 Part 1.

Note that after you've recharacterized it as a Traditional IRA contribution, you can also then ""convert"" that Traditional IRA money to a Roth IRA if you want, achieving the same state as what you have now. Contributing to a Traditional IRA and then converting to a Roth IRA is called a ""backdoor Roth IRA contribution""; if you don't have any existing pre-tax money in Traditional IRA or other IRAs, then this achieves the same as a regular Roth IRA contribution except with no income limits.
